Rocher Foundation opens its next postdoctoral fellowship round in classical Indology

The two-year fellowship, held at a host institution in the United States, pays a stipend of at least $80,000 a year to a recent PhD in classical Indology. Applications close on 15 January 2027.

Talaash Heritage desk · Published 19 November 2026

Where
United States
Apply by
15 January 2027

The Ludo and Rosane Rocher Foundation is taking applications for its next round of postdoctoral fellowships in classical Indology. Applications can be sent at any time up to 15 January 2027, and the foundation says results will be announced to applicants on or about 1 April 2027.

The foundation sets the scope widely. It covers texts and related sources, usually from before the 19th century, in Sanskrit, Prakrit, Pali, early Dravidian languages and other premodern Indian languages, as well as languages of the wider cultural world they reached, such as Persian and Kawi. Related arts and material culture, and the history of Indology itself, also count.

Applicants need a doctorate, typically a PhD or DPhil, in a relevant field of classical Indology from an accredited university in any country, completed within five years before the fellowship begins. Every requirement for the degree, including the dissertation defence, must be finished by 15 January 2027. The fellowship is meant for revising a dissertation into publishable form, for starting a new project after the doctorate, or both.

The fellowship lasts up to 24 months, starting at the beginning of an academic session at the host institution. The stipend is at least $80,000 a year, or the host's own postdoctoral rate if that is higher. The second year depends on a satisfactory first-year progress report and a letter from the host agreeing to continue.

Fellows must be in residence at a university or research institution in the United States. Applicants propose one or more sponsors in their application, with the department, programme or mentor, and the foundation advises contacting them first. The host is normally not the institution that awarded the doctorate, and it cannot be one where the applicant has served as faculty. Fellows are encouraged to teach one course and give at least one lecture a year. The 2026 fellow, Radha Blinderman, is at Brown University preparing a critical edition, translation and study of part of Balarāma's Prabodhaprakāśa, an 18th-century Sanskrit grammar; the foundation says the work bears on the history of Bengal.
